Sessions, resumption and forking.
This is task statement one point seven: manage session state, resumption, and forking.
By the end of this part, you'll know when to resume, when to fork, when to start fresh, and how to recover from a crash without leaning on a transcript.
Let's start with a picture.
Come back to a half-finished job after a week away.
Your notes are both the reason you can pick it up, and the reason you can get it badly wrong.
The notes record exactly what you believed when you put them down.
They say nothing about the fact that somebody tidied the room.
Or that the ladder you left against the wall has been borrowed.
You act on the notes with total confidence.
Because from your point of view, no time has passed.
A saved session is that notebook.
It holds the conversation.
What was said.
What was found.
What was decided.
It holds nothing about the world those statements were about.
And there's a second move worth knowing.
Before trying an alternative approach, you can scribble the new plan over the page you have.
Or you can photocopy the page, and scribble on the copy.
The copy costs almost nothing, and keeps the original safe.
But here the analogy has a sharp edge.
Photocopying the notebook gives you two notebooks.
And there's still only one room.
Two plans acting on the same room still collide.
The technical version.
The SDK writes each session to disk as you work.
As JSONL files under ~/.claude/projects/, in a folder named after the encoded working directory.
There are three ways back in.
One at a time.
One. continue.
It's spelled continue: true in TypeScript, and continue_conversation=True in Python.
It picks up the most recent session in the current directory, with no id to track.
Two. resume.
It takes a specific session id, captured from session_id on the result message.
It's what you need when several conversations run at once.
Three. fork_session in Python, or forkSession in TypeScript, used together with resume.
It creates a new session that starts with a copy of the original's history, and diverges from there.
In Claude Code, the same three appear as claude --continue, claude --resume, and --fork-session, or the /branch command.
The distinction the exam probes.
continue and resume both add to an existing session.
So its history grows.
Fork copies the history into a new session id.
And it leaves the original untouched.
And the caveat the exam loves most.
The documentation says sessions persist the conversation, not the filesystem.
And forking branches the conversation history, not the filesystem.
So if a forked agent edits files, those changes are real.
And they're visible to any session working in the same directory.
Hold on to this line.
Resumption restores what the agent knew, not what is now true.
Question one.
Here's the scenario.
A developer spent ninety minutes in a named Claude Code session, building an analysis of a large service for a refactoring plan.
Two days later, they return to continue.
Meanwhile, only two files changed: auth.py and stripe_handler.py.
Both were edited by a colleague.
What should they do?
Take a second.
You return from a week's leave to a half-finished kitchen renovation.
A colleague says only the sink and the tap were changed while you were away.
So you re-check those two, and carry on.
You wouldn't rip out the whole kitchen.
And you wouldn't assume nothing changed.
The answer.
Resume the session, and state which two files changed.
Tell it not to rely on earlier results for them.
When context is still largely valid, and the changes are few and known, resume plus an explicit change notice keeps the expensive baseline.
And it triggers targeted re-analysis.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: resume and continue directly, trusting the agent to notice.
Why?
The agent can't detect external file changes on its own.
It trusts its transcript.
And it may act on old contents.
That's the named anti-pattern of treating resume as a time machine.
Wrong: fork the session, so the updated files are handled separately.
Why?
Forking is for exploring alternatives, not for handling file updates over time.
Wrong: start fresh, and redo the whole analysis.
Why?
That throws away ninety minutes of still-valid work, over two files.
Hold on to this line.
Resume when the old context is mostly still true.
And tell the agent exactly what changed.
Question two.
This one is pick two.
Here's the scenario.
An architect has a session holding a costly two-hour exploration of a monolith.
They want to compare two migration strategies, serverless and containerised, from that shared baseline.
Both will involve trial edits to files.
They want the original session left intact.
And neither strategy's edits contaminating the other.
Which two?
Take a second.
Two architects photocopy the same site survey, to sketch competing designs.
Cheap, and the original stays clean.
But if both start knocking down walls in the one real building, their plans collide.
Copies of the notes still need separate models of the building.
The answers.
First.
Fork the baseline session once per strategy.
So each gets a new session id, with a copy of the history.
Second.
Give each fork its own working copy of the code.
Why?
Because forks branch the conversation, not the filesystem.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: resume the baseline for the first strategy, then resume it again for the second.
Why?
Resuming appends.
So the first strategy gets welded into the history the second would start from.
Wrong: start two fresh sessions, and redo the exploration in each.
Why?
That pays twice for work a fork shares almost for free.
And the key trap.
Wrong: rely on the fork to isolate file edits, because each fork keeps a private copy of the repository.
Why?
It doesn't.
The notes add one more thing.
An in-session fork in Claude Code is especially cheap.
Its system prompt and tool definitions match the parent's.
So its first request reuses the parent's prompt cache.

There's a matching one in the notes.
Here's the scenario.
An engineer tried a different fix by resuming the same session with a new prompt.
Two hours later, the original thread was no longer usable.
What should they have done?
Take a second.
The answer. fork_session with resume.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: start fresh.
Why?
That throws away context.
Wrong: continue.
Why? continue appends, just like resume.
Wrong: file checkpointing.
Why?
It's the wrong subsystem.
It snapshots file changes, not conversations.
Hold on to this line.
Fork to explore.
Resume to continue.
And give each fork its own copy of the files.
Question four.
Here's the scenario.
A weekly security audit in continuous integration resumes last week's session, to avoid re-reading the repository.
This week, a large restructuring moved or deleted hundreds of files.
The resumed agent confidently reports vulnerabilities at line numbers, in files that no longer exist.
The team still wants to benefit from last week's findings.
What's the fix?
Take a second.
An inspector returns to a building that was gutted and rebuilt since last year.
Reading last year's report aloud as if it still applied would be dangerous.
Instead, they carry last year's list as things to check.
They walk the new building.
And they confirm or strike each item.
The answer.
In exam terms, when prior tool results are fundamentally stale, resuming is counterproductive.
Start a fresh session.
Inject last week's findings as a structured summary, framed explicitly as hypotheses to validate.
Not facts.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: keep resuming, with a note that the repository changed a lot.
Why?
A vague note can't correct hundreds of stale file and line references the transcript still asserts.
Wrong: fork last week's session.
Why?
A fork copies the same stale history into a new id, and isolates nothing.
Wrong: resume with a larger context window, and re-read everything on top.
Why?
It keeps the stale transcript.
It adds cost.
And it doesn't tell the agent which beliefs are wrong.
So here's the three-way contrast, which the exam loves.
Resume, with an explicit change notice, when the context is still largely valid, and the changes are few and known.
Fork, when you want to compare alternatives from a costly baseline without disturbing it.
Remembering that the files are shared.
Start fresh with an injected summary, framed as hypotheses, when the world has changed so much that the old transcript is more misleading than useful.
Now crash recovery.
That's a different problem again.
In plain words, if a long job dies halfway, you want it to pick up where it left off.
Not start over.
The tempting answer is to save the transcript, and resume it.
The better answer is to write down, as you go, the small set of facts you'd want on a clean start.
The documentation is direct about this.
Don't rely on session resume.
Capture the results you need, such as analysis output, decisions and file diffs, as application state.
And pass them into a fresh session's prompt.
Why?
Session files are local to the machine that created them.
That's fatal on containers that get recycled, or on serverless hosts.
There are two supported ways to keep transcripts anyway.
One.
Attach a sessionStore adapter, spelled session_store in Python.
It mirrors transcripts to your own backend, keyed on the working directory.
Two.
Move the JSONL file yourself.
Both are heavier than writing down what you learned.
Question five.
The notes have the scenario.
Here's the scenario.
A nightly job audits forty microservice repositories, one subagent each.
The container is preemptible, and recycles about twice a week.
And every time, the next run starts from repository one.
The team proposes persisting transcripts to object storage, and resuming.
What's the strongest design?
Take a second.
The answer.
A structured state record.
Let me take its parts one at a time.
One.
One addressable unit per repository.
Two.
A status written before each attempt, as well as after.
So a unit killed mid-audit is distinguishable from one never started.
Three.
A bounded attempt count.
Three per unit in the notes, which is a house number, rather than a platform limit.
So a unit that fails deterministically is abandoned, instead of retried until the budget dies.
Four.
The locked decisions.
So a resumed run stays consistent.
Five.
Artifact addresses, rather than contents.
So the record stays small.
Six.
An atomic write.
So the crash you're recovering from can't leave a half-written state file.
And on restart, skip every unit already marked done.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: the session store, or the copied transcript.
Why?
Both work in principle.
But they're heavier, and more fragile.
Wrong: raise maxTurns and maxBudgetUsd.
Why?
That doesn't address recovery at all.
It just makes each run longer, and more likely to be interrupted.
One last mechanic.
Sessions don't give you a way to undo file changes.
If file changes must be revertible, use file checkpointing.
And pin the working directory, so the session lookup and the checkout agree.
The context management chapter returns to the idea of extracting durable facts before they're summarised away.
That's part seven.
If you remember one thing, make it this.
A session remembers the conversation, not the world.
Resume with a change notice when little has changed.
Fork to explore, with separate copies of the files.
Start fresh with hypotheses when a lot has changed.
And recover from crashes with a small state record, not a transcript.
